Run a plan

Source: R/run_plan.R
run_plan.Rd

run_plan() runs every analysis of the plnr plan p, in this R session or on workers new R sessions. It stops the run at the first failed analysis, and then it prints each failed analysis with its error.

Usage

run_plan(p, workers = 1)

Arguments

p

A plan from plnr::Plan$new(), with data from add_data() and analyses from add_analyses().

workers

The number of R sessions that run the analyses, one whole number of 1 or more.

Value

Invisibly, a named list with one element for each analysis of the plan, in the order of the plan. Element i is the value of the action function of analysis i. Give it to save_results().

Details

With workers = 1, run_plan() calls p$run_all() in this R session.

With workers 2 or more, run_plan() needs the packages future and doFuture. It starts a PSOCK cluster of workers new R sessions with parallel::makePSOCKcluster(). It runs p$run_all() with the foreach path of plnr, on doFuture::registerDoFuture() with the future plan future::cluster on that cluster. A PSOCK cluster does not fork, so it also works on Windows. Each future runs a batch of tasks of plnr on a worker, and each task holds the analyses that get the data of one key. Each worker gets about 4 batches when each data function with arguments has both scenario and sim, or when no data function has arguments. Otherwise each task is a batch of its own.

Each worker starts with the library paths of this R session, from .libPaths(). While it starts the cluster, run_plan() sets the environment variable R_LIBS to these paths, and then it sets R_LIBS back. So a worker also finds a library that this R session added with .libPaths(), for example the temporary library of R CMD build. Each worker runs with 1 thread. While run_plan() starts the cluster, it sets the environment variables OMP_NUM_THREADS, OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS and MKL_NUM_THREADS to 1, as it sets R_LIBS. Then it sets them back in this R session. OpenMP and the BLAS libraries OpenBLAS and MKL read them when they start their threads, so the variables MUST be there when the worker starts. The section One thread for each worker gives the rules.

Before the run, run_plan() gives each worker these:

  • the library paths of this R session again, with .libPaths().

  • 1 thread: the three variables again, for a library that the worker loads later, and data.table::setDTthreads(1) when data.table is installed.

  • the packages attached in this R session, in the order of search(), for example data.table after library(data.table) in the run script.

  • the kind of random number generator of this R session, from RNGkind().

  • the paths in org::project, such as org::project$home.

  • the folders of initialize_project(), so that folder() works on the worker. A worker then loads pbn.

A future starts with an empty global environment. initialize_project() sources the functions folder into an environment, .GlobalEnv by default. Each batch takes every object of that environment to the global environment of its worker. A data function and an action function then find CFG and the other functions of the folder. A plnr plan and .Random.seed are left out. Each batch takes a copy of each object, so keep large objects out of that environment.

run_plan() does not copy the R options, for example options(digits = 3), and no other state of this R session. A future sets the option mc.cores to 1. run_plan() removes it on a worker, so parallel::mclapply() in an analysis uses its default number of cores. The output, the messages and the warnings of a worker come to this R session at the end of each batch.

After the run, run_plan() stops the cluster and registers the sequential foreach backend, also after an error. It sets the future plan and the option doFuture.rng.onMisuse back to their values before the run. Each data function and each analysis sets its own seed, so run_plan() turns off the warning of doFuture about random numbers for the run. plnr calls each data function once for each scenario and simulation, see add_data(). Each data function and each analysis sets its own seed before it runs, see add_analyses(). Take a function that depends only on its arguments, the objects of the functions folder such as CFG, the attached packages and the seed. Its results with workers = 1 and with workers = 2 are identical(). A function that reads an R option or another state of the main R session can give other results on a worker. A data.table loses its self-reference on the way back from a worker, and run_plan() gives it a new one with data.table::setalloccol(). It does this for each data.table in a value or in a plain list in a value, at any depth. It does not do this for a data.table in a list column of a data.frame. Such a value MAY differ in identical() between 1 worker and more.

An error in an action function fails that analysis, and an error in a data function fails each analysis that gets the data. pbn saves no results of a run with a failed analysis, so the first failed analysis stops the run. The section Stop at the first failure gives the rules. After the run, run_plan() prints each failed analysis with its name and its full error message with cat(), and then it stops. R cuts an error message at 1000 bytes by default, and cat() does not. The error message of run_plan() gives the number of failed analyses and of the analyses that did not run. It also names the first failed analysis in the order of the plan, and holds its error. pbn cuts that error to keep the message below 900 bytes. When 2 or more analyses fail and all have the same error, the message says so. The results files of an earlier run stay as they are. After initialize_project(), run_plan() writes the run log <version>_results/run.md with the failures before it stops. The section The run log of save_results() describes it.

After initialize_project(), run_plan() first replaces the run log with one that says that the run has not finished, and deletes the errors file <version>_results/run_errors_gitexclude.md. A call of run_plan() without save_results() after it leaves this log.

run_plan() measures the elapsed time of each data step and of each analysis where it runs, also on a worker, and the time of the clock of the computer at its end. The times go to the record of the plan, and save_results() writes them to the run log. They are not in the value, so two runs stay identical().

The value carries the attribute pbn_run, a stamp of the plan. It holds no count of the runs, so two runs of one plan can be identical(). save_results() stops on a value without the stamp of its plan.

run_plan() sets use_foreach of the plan: FALSE for 1 worker and TRUE for more.

After initialize_project(), run_plan() first lists the files of the folders of the project again, with their sizes and modification times. It reads no content of a file. The value carries this fingerprint in its stamp, and save_results() writes it to manifest$data_files.

An analysis that changes the shared data or an object of the functions folder in place fails. An analysis that leaves a new object in the global environment fails too. add_analyses() gives the rules.

An error outside the wrappers of pbn ends the run. Examples are a worker that stops, and an error of plnr or of the backend of the workers. run_plan() then prints the whole error, and writes the run log with it after initialize_project(). It stops with one message that holds the error, cut below 900 bytes, and saves nothing. The future plan, the foreach backend and the options go back as after any run, and the cluster stops.

For a data function with cache = TRUE, run_plan() needs initialize_project() first, and it prints one line for each scenario and simulation. The section Cache of add_data() gives the rules. A data function that returns a cohort::CohortPipeline runs on the worker, and only its data.table and its exclusion table come back. The section A cohort as the data of add_data() gives the rules.

One thread for each worker

Some packages start threads of their own, for example data.table, fixest, a threaded BLAS and OpenMP code. By default, such a package uses many cores. data.table, for example, uses half of the cores of the computer. With workers 2 or more, each worker would do that, and the computer would run far more threads than cores. So run_plan() makes each worker use 1 thread. There is no argument to change it. An analysis that needs more threads in its worker sets them in its own code, for example data.table::setDTthreads(4) at the top of its action function.

With workers = 1, run_plan() changes no thread setting, and the analyses run with the settings of this R session.

The results of the test projects of pbn are identical() with 1 and 2 workers. pbn does not check this for other code. A threaded BLAS MAY sum in another order with another number of threads. So a matrix product of such a BLAS MAY differ in its last digits between workers = 1 and more workers. With 1 worker it has the threads of this R session, and with more it has 1 thread.

Stop at the first failure

A failed data function makes each analysis of its scenario and simulation fail, and save_results() needs a run without a failed analysis. So no analysis after the first failure can give a result, and run_plan() stops the run there. There is no option to run on. These are the rules:

  • After the first failed analysis, no new data function and no new analysis starts. An analysis whose data failed fails at once, also after the stop, without a call of its action function.

  • With 1 worker, the stop comes directly after the failed analysis.

  • With workers, the failed analysis creates a folder in the temporary folder of this R session. Each worker looks for it before each data function, and at most every 0.5 seconds before an analysis. pbn does not stop an analysis that runs. So the longest delay is the rest of the longest analysis that runs at the time of the failure, plus 0.5 seconds. The batches that did not start still go to the workers, and each of them ends at once.

  • Each analysis that did not run counts as not run. It is not a failure.

The display shows the stop at once, and the run log says that the run stopped early and how many analyses did not run.

Progress

run_plan() shows one line for each scenario: its finished analyses of all its analyses, the failed ones among them, the time since its start, and a note. The note is one of these:

  • "waiting" before the scenario starts, and "done" at its end.

  • "stopping" after the first failed analysis of the run, and "stopped early" with the analyses that did not run at the end.

  • the last text of progress() from an analysis of the scenario, while that analysis runs.

  • otherwise the time left, from the analyses of the scenario that ended without a failure, after at least 3 and at least 10% of them.

The analyses that count the rows do not count. The display replaces the progress bar of plnr. The header of the display in a terminal gives the time since the start of the run. So does the start of each line of a log, for example pbn: [12m 05s] null 522/1200 analyses, 8m 53s, about 12m left.

In an interactive terminal, the display draws its lines again in place. In RStudio and in another console without ANSI codes, it draws one line again in place. It shows the lines of each scenario at the end. While the display is shown, progressr holds back other output, messages and warnings, and shows them above it.

Without an interactive session, for example with Rscript into a log, in knitr and in testthat, the display only adds lines:

  • nothing in the first 60 seconds of the run, other than the line of the first failed analysis. A short run without a failure adds no line.

  • one line at once when the first analysis fails, also in the first 60 seconds.

  • after 60 seconds, a header, and one line for each scenario that started.

  • one line when a scenario finishes.

  • one line for a running scenario at most every 60 seconds. The line comes only when 10% more of the scenario is done, in analyses or in its last text of progress().

A worker sends the count of its finished analyses at most every 0.5 seconds, and at the end of each scenario and simulation. The display uses progressr with a handler of its own, inside progressr::with_progress(). It sets no progressr handler of the R session, so the handlers that another package sets stay as they are.

See also

vignette("pbn"), which builds and runs a small fake project.

Other plan: add_analyses(), add_data(), cohort_data(), get_data(), progress()

Examples

CFG <- list(scenarios = data.frame(scenario = c("real", "null"), sims = 2))
p <- plnr::Plan$new()
pbn::add_data(p, "d", fn = function(scenario, sim) {
  return(data.frame(x = stats::rnorm(5)))
})
pbn::add_analyses(
  p,
  pbn::scenarios(CFG),
  name = "mean_x",
  fn = function(data, argset) return(data.frame(mean = mean(data$d$x)))
)
r <- pbn::run_plan(p)
r[["null__sim_0002__mean_x__1"]]
#>          mean
#> 1 -0.06696949
